content.title: The nonconvex analysis should be presented and baselines need to be improved.
content.review:
This paper is a lack of theoritical guarantees. The authors do not present any  soild theoretical guarantee for the proposed algorithms and any solid insight. The convergence rersults directly use  previous convex analysis. The nonconvex results are missing.
The experiments  are all toy tasks and the baseline was deliberately lowered. For example, Resnet20 used SGD with momentum 300 epoches to achieve 93% accuracy.    For the PTB experiment, Adam train LSTM's Perplexity can easily reach 60, and their report is more than 88. The results in this paper do not match existing SOTAS.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper. First, we would like to express our disappointment, as the title of the review states that we DELIBERATELY lowered the baselines in the experiments, implying that we provide false results, and that we cherry-picked our findings. We are willing to share code with the reviewer (unanonimously) of the settings we ran.

Nevertheless, we would like to politely request for any concrete suggestions for improvement. We're not really sure what kind of theoretical guarantees you are looking for beyond what is presented in this paper, which is on par, or beyond, a typical deep learning optimization paper. We provide insights for our proposal + convergence rate guarantees for convex scenarios. As we claim, in a previous response to another reviewer, the proof for the non-convex case can be found in another paper, where the sequence of beta_t's is not defined, but only assumed that beta_t < 1, for all t.

We also do not understand your sentiment of toy tasks. We've provided results on MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, Tiny ImageNet, Penn Treebank (PTB); with ResNets,  Wide-ResNets, VGG-16, LSTMs, VAEs, Capsule networks, and Noise Conditional Score Network (NCSN). Could you perhaps provide some indication of why you believe these are toy tasks for deep learning optimization? 

Some stats regarding deliberately lowered baseline performance: For ResNet20 with SGDM see the popular github repo (https://github.com/akamaster/pytorch\_resnet\_cifar10 or https://github.com/yihui-he/resnet-cifar10-caffe or https://github.com/twtygqyy/resnet-cifar10) which are the first three github repos on Google if you search Resnet 20 cifar 10. These actually typically claim 8.5\% test error, which is higher than this paper. ResNet 20 is commonly conflated with ResNet 18 which is a different network that achieves a slightly lower test error. And for LSTM we used the official tensorflow v1 implementation for LSTM-PTB which you can download here https://github.com/tensorflow/models/releases/tag/v1.11 . In some cases, stronger data augmentation or other tricks can be used to boost performance, however this is a deep learning optimization paper so it is fair as long as these are held constant.

content.title: Another reviewer's take
content.comment:
I also agree that strong theoretical results aren't needed in an optimization for DL paper. Assuming otherwise most often leads to a lot of [nonsense math](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03341) that doesn't serve any elucidating purpose, and I'm actually relieved that the authors chose to omit the usual frivolous theorems that I've encountered in the rest of my review load.

That said, I do think it is a fair criticism that the baselines can be easily strengthened. The choice of ResNet20 in this sort of paper is fairly unconventional. Assuming Demon is a robust decay schedule, we should be able to see some benefits with ResNet18s with the standard 30-60-90 schedule, and I would encourage the authors to incorporate those results in lieu of ResNet20. Such a showing does not require significantly more compute.

I don't have a great sense of "standard practices" for PTB, but there are certain data augmentation practices for CIFAR10 and ImageNet models that have become conventional (e.g. cropping/flipping strategies). If there are similarly routine and widely-accepted practices for PTB models, then I would strongly encourage the authors to adopt them.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments and suggestions: we have updated results with ResNet18 below:

ResNet18 w/ 30-60-90 LR Decay: 6.06 +- 0.07

ResNet18 w/ Demon: 5.59 +- 0.12

Performance with Demon is consistently strong, and it should come as no surprise that it works here too.

We are not experts in NLP, which is why we leaned on the official TensorFlow implementation for the PTB-LSTM task. We use standard augmentations for the CV tasks.

content.title: Non-convex convergence result for Demon
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer,

To answer your request, here is the convergence proof of Demon for the case of Adam (note: this is the more difficult case than the simpler SGD+M+Demon case):

Theorem: Assuming $\tau \in \\{1, 2, \dots, T\\}$ is an index over $T$ iterations, Demon + Adam satisfies

$\mathbb{E}[ \\|\nabla f(x_{\tau})\\|_2^{4/3} ]^{3/2}  \leq \frac{C + C' \\sum_t \alpha_t \sqrt\{1 - \theta_t\}}{\alpha_T \cdot T} = O(\frac{1}{T})$

where $C, C'$ are constants, $\alpha_t$ are step sizes, $\theta_t$ are the parameters related to the diagonal Hessian approximation of Adam's preconditioner, and $\beta_t < 1$, as is the case for Demon technique. 

Moreover, one can remove the expectation requirement above, and have the same result hold deterministically with some probability $1 - \delta^{2/3}$:

$\\|\nabla f(x_{\tau})\\|_2^2 \leq \frac{C + C' \\sum_t \alpha_t \sqrt\{1 - \theta_t\}}{\delta \cdot \alpha_T \cdot T} = O(\frac{1}{T})$.

To achieve the above, the assumptions are lower-bounded function $f$, $L$-smoothness, and standard assumptions on gradients. Regarding the parameters, momentum $\beta_t$ has to satisfy $0 \leq \beta_t \leq \beta < 1$, for some $\beta$: *this is exactly the setting of Demon, where $\beta$ is the initial value of the momentum, and $\beta_t$ decreases to zero.*

The reason we do not state this result explicitly is because we point the readers to the paper: "A Sufficient Condition for Convergences of Adam and RMSProp" that is accepted in CVPR 2019. And we state that explicitly in the first sentences of our proof. But, if we repeated the proof this would lead to plagiarism to existing literature. Our work is an exact instance of decreasing momentum that leads to significant improvements compared to previous work; to the best of our knowledge, no other paper has considered a specific decreasing schedule for momentum that is at the same time almost "hyperparameter-free". 

We re-state the argument/theory here. We believe we have answered ALL reviewer's comments, but nevertheless we are still on the "reject" side.

content.title: Decaying momentum helps training of deep networks
content.review:
Authors propose a decaying schedule of momentum. Using the enchancement and applying to Adam, the authors see that better performance overall, less sensitive to hyperparameters.

Reason to score:

This idea is interesting on its on. It adds a dependency on momentum to total steps T to train on. Emperical evidence show a small improvement over baselines, hence this suggests that this of practical use. 

I have listed my concerns below and hopefully authors can address my concern during the rebuttal period.

Concerns/Questions:

Comparisons with averaging and related methods can improve the paper.
 Is it an averaging effect that we see in models when reducing the learning rate to zero? This will answer where the improvements (2-5%) come from, the results indicate that this might be going on, as there is a sharp improvement during the end of training as momentum is decayed.

a) Could you compare the method with one in "Reducing the variance in online optimization by transporting past gradients", S Arnold et al https://papers.nips.cc/paper/8779-reducing-the-variance-in-online-optimization-by-transporting-past-gradients.pdf

b) How well does baselines, experiment improvement when polyak averaging or stochastic weight averaging is enabled.

Claims in Appendix: D LINEAR REGRESSION is problematic

a) would authors clarify what theory they refer to?
b) experiments indicate that SGD, SGD-M, and SGD-Deamon all perform the same? Did the authors mean to do full-batch training there?

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review this paper and we appreciate the comments.

"Comparisons with ... is decayed."

We agree and believe that this further analysis is an exciting future direction of Demon; we are aware of the work from Francis Bach, Simon Lacoste-Julien, Nicolas Le Roux, etc on stochastic averaging optimization methods. However, we believe that this analysis is outside the scope of the current paper, as we are targeting well-established optimizers in DL (e.g., for the paper you mention later on in your review, i) we were not aware of it, ii) in that paper, there is no comparison beyond SGD and Adam, while we are way extensive and we show we are clearly better in many scenarios). We've tried to compare with a large array of optimizers (Adam, AMSGrad, QHAdam, YellowFin, SGDM, Aggmo, QHM, and in the appendix OneCycle, effective learning rate adjusted SGD, Padam, various other momentum schedules). We hope the reviewer will appreciate our research direction that goes extensively beyond any similar efforts on the same subject.

"a) Could you compare ... -by-transporting-past-gradients.pdf"

Thanks for the reference - this is an interesting paper and we've added this as a citation. As mentioned above, we've included many methods that it would be unwieldy to the reader to add more. We can try to repeat some of our settings on the algorithms proposed in that paper, and compare with Demon. However, we can only append the results in the appendix of the final version. Thanks again for the reference - it is a great paper.

"b) How well does ... stochastic weight averaging is enabled."

See further above addressing weight averaging.

"Claims in Appendix: D ... full-batch training there?"

The purpose of that section in the appendix is to handle some TCS algorithms as in:

On the insufficiency of existing momentum schemes for Stochastic Optimization, by Rahul Kidambi, Praneeth Netrapalli, Prateek Jain, and Sham M. Kakade.

Following that paper, in the linear regression setting, samples are drawn from a distribution, so there isn't a concept of full-batch training. This is a cornercase toy example, where the above papers show the suboptimality of the heavy ball method. We demonstrate that even though the convergence bound for Demon SGDM in Appendix C is not as tight as SGDM, the convergence rate is preserved. Moreover, our results highlight that using momentum as in Demon in stochastic settings do not show any problems, compared to the behavior shown in the above paper of plain use of momentum in SGD.

content.title: Well-written paper but is this just linear decay?
content.review:
# Summary

### Demon schedule

This paper proposes a momentum schedule for gradient-based optimization called "Demon". The functional form of the momentum schedule is:
$$
  \beta_t = \beta_0 \frac{1 - t / T}{(1 - \beta_0) + \beta_0 (1 - t / T)}
$$

The motivation is intuitive rather than theoretical ("Demon is motivated by learning rate decay models which reduce the impact of a gradient to current and future updates"). The authors' notation is a bit imprecise, but I believe that the specific functional form arises from the paper's implicit observation that for any value of $\beta_t$, the total contribution of that momentum term is:
$$
  \sum_{i = t}^T \prod_{j = t}^{i - t} \beta_{t + j}
$$
which the paper claims converges to $\beta / (1 - \beta)$ as $T \rightarrow \infty$. Thus, to simulate an effect similar to learning rate decay, the paper solves for:
$$
  \frac{\beta_t}{1 - \beta_t} = (1 - t / T) \frac{\beta_0}{1 - \beta_0}
$$

The solution is the paper's proposed functional form.

### Empirical analysis

The paper proposes to apply the above schedule to momentum SGD and Adam. The paper lists a wide range of evaluation scenarios, including CIFAR, Tiny Imagenet, STL10, PTB, and (F)MNIST. In the "mainline" experiments, the tuned hyperparameter is learning rate and all other hyperparameters are fixed.

In the context of the paper's experimental setup, the results show that (1) for a given value of $\beta$, using Demon allows the user a wider range of admissible learning rates, and (2) the Demon schedule results in consistently lower error upon convergence than a fixed momentum.

# Merits of the paper

The experimental results are striking and hold over many different environments.

Moreover, the paper is clear that the proposed schedule comes from an intuitive motivation rather than some contrived pseudo-mathy derivation. I can't thank the authors enough for doing so. It is so refreshing to see a paper that plainly states "we thought of something, we tried it, and it works." The paper shows benefits above and beyond linear momentum decay, which justifies the somewhat unconventional functional form that is derived.

The paper's convergence results are welcome but the authors wisely choose to elaborate in the appendix as the convergence of the algorithms should be immediately evident to a reader working in this field.

# Drawbacks

Two unresolved questions jump to mind:

- **To what extent is momentum decay interchangeable with learning rate decay?** That is, how much of the Demon decay schedule's benefits actually come from the momentum decay component, versus the indirect effect of reducing update magnitudes? To answer this question, I would like to see a set of experiments which hold momentum fixed at $\beta = 0.9$ and instead reduce the learning rate to achieve the same decay in update magnitude. I haven't worked out the math to figure out what this would look like, but the authors are welcome to follow up with a proposed LR schedule and I will verify.
- **Are the authors' PTB results rigorous and is the baseline configuration appropriate?** I will rely on other reviewers' assessment as I am not an NLP practitioner myself. I'm not looking for SOTA here, simply that the paper's configuration is commonly accepted as a baseline.

# Overall Rating

My original rating was a 4 due to reviewer math error. After correcting for the error and examining the authors' updated results, my initial score is a 6. I may adjust depending on further discussion or new results.

# Comments / points of clarification

- "Moreover, for an asymptotically large number of iterations, we know that $\beta$ contributes on up to $t − 1$ terms." This statement is unclear.
- While I don't believe this is significant enough to discuss in detail in the Drawbacks section, the argument that the sum of $\beta$ contributions converges to $\beta / (1 - \beta)$ is a bit of a stretch given that $\beta_t$ is non-constant. It is probably fine in the limit but the authors should discuss and justify this approximation explicitly in the paper.
- I gather that "exploration" refers to CIFAR and STL, while "mainline" refers to all other experiments. However, the paper does not actually define the delineation between "exploration" and "mainline", so it would be great to revise accordingly.
- Where possible, the empirical analysis should be expanded to do head-to-head comparisons. For example, instead of comparing SGD-Demon and Adam-Demon with AdamW, AMSGrad, QHM, QHAdam, you could do "AdamW-Demon" vs. "AdamW", and so on.

# Retracted comments

The comments below were in the original version of the review but are incorrect. I am preserving them here for transparency.

My suspicion is that the paper's proposed schedule is an overly complex form of the the following: $\beta_t = \beta_0 (1 - t / T)$. Here are some example plots: [0.999](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=graph+%281+-+x%29+%2F+%280.999+%2B+0.001+%281+-+x%29%29+from+0+to+1), [0.9](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=graph+%281+-+x%29+%2F+%280.9+%2B+0.1+%281+-+x%29%29+from+0+to+1), and [0.8](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=graph+%281+-+x%29+%2F+%280.8+%2B+0.2+%281+-+x%29%29+from+0+to+1). Unless there is a compelling reason (or the authors can show significantly better results of their schedule over linear decay), then this paper should instead just be an empirical analysis of linearly decayed momentum.

In this light, I do believe there are some overreach concerns with the paper's present claims. I would like to see one of the following:

- Results across the experimental suite showing that the Demon schedule is better than linear momentum decay.
- A re-scoping of the paper's stated contributions as follows: "We perform the first large-scale empirical analysis of linear momentum decay and find ..."

My overall rating is a 4 as written, due to the significance concerns. I don't think this paper can survive as a "here's a novel momentum schedule" paper given its likely similarity to linear decay. However, I'm of the opinion that a large-scale, well-executed empirical analysis of linear momentum decay is relevant and useful to the ICLR audience. I am willing to increase my score if the paper is re-scoped as such (or if the authors can demonstrate a real difference from linear decay).

My rating does not reflect my admiration of the authors' work. This is a well-written paper with results that, presented in the appropriate form, deserve an audience.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you so much for taking the time to review the paper and we appreciate the comments.

"Results across ... better than linear momentum decay."

In the updated version of the text we've included preliminary experiments comparing Demon schedule with other schedules. Linear decay was the first thing we tried, but attained worse results so we didn't pursue it much further or include it initially in the paper. See Table 18 in Appendix G for linear decay and other decay schedules. There is also a plot in the paper showing the Demon schedule (see Figure 1). We would like to emphasize that Demon is very different than a linear momentum decay schedule. Given that this is the main reason for "Reject", we hope a significant upgrade of our score, unless more issues are presented by the reviewer. 

"A re-scoping ... and find ..."

This is a good idea and we've rewritten parts of our contribution with some edits. To clarify, a linear momentum decay performs worse than the Demon schedule. Given that we have already made changes to reflect reviewer's comment, this comment should be considered resolved. We really thank the reviewer for such constructive comments.

"Moreover, ... is unclear"

We will clarify this in the paper.

"While I don't ... explicitly in the paper."
 
We have a short section at the end of Motivation and interpretation discussing this and we would be happy to provide additional support, but for most realistic cases, besides extremely large batch training, the approximation is so close that it can't be identified visually.

"I gather ... revise accordingly."

We will emphasize this, but we also point out that this exists in the original text ("The exploration setting (CIFAR10/100/STL10, and following general guidelines in literature) informed our settings for other experiments.") in the second paragraph of Section 5.

"Where possible, ... vs. "AdamW", and so on."

Given the empirical results, we are confident that it extends to other optimizers, but we compare primarily with SGDM and Adam since they are the most well established optimizers, and also to avoid bloating the paper with too many results.

Again, many thanks to the reviewer for the comments, and we are appreciated that our work is considered clear and helpful through its simplicity.

content.title: The topic of this paper is interesting
content.review:
Overall, the paper is well-organized and easy to understand. The authors proposed a new momentum decay strategy  for SGDM and Adam methods, experimental results shown the effectiveness of the propsoed methods. I have the following comments/questions.

1. The motivation of using $\beta_t$ is still not clear to me. Could you please explain more?

2. The convergence analysis is in the convex setting, which does not satisfy neural network training. I do not think the proposed methods have theoretical guarantee in training neural network. It would be better if the convergence rate can be established in the non-convex setting. I am happy to see if the authors can provide the new analysis for non-convex setting.

3. The proposed Demon methods require knowing the value of total iterations T before running it, which is different from SGD and its variants such as SGDM and Adam. This is quite similar to SGDM with cosine decay learning rate. Another question is that why don't you compare with SGDM with cosine decay learning rate in the experiments? I would like to see if the authors can show such results. 

4. The authors claimed that "DEMON momentum SGD is observed to be significantly less sensitive to parameter tuning than momentum SGD with learning rate decay schedule". Could you please show the evidence in experiments?
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

replying_to: Replying to The topic of this paper is interesting

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper and we appreciate the comments.

"The motivation ... explain more?"

The main motivation is similar to that of learning rate decay, which is primarily (among other objectives) to reduce the impact of a gradient to current and future updates. We propose to do so with Demon, a momentum decay algorithm. Moreover, and in contrast to learning rate decay that has non-intuitive "breakpoints" to decrease learning rate, Demon has a decaying rule that stays the same for every case we have tried (meaning that it is not fully optimized for each individual case), leading to less a intensive hyperparameter tuning process.

"The convergence non-convex setting."

In the paper, we've explicitly provided a reference to a non-convex work, under which Demon can be reparameterized. We didn't write out the proof because the reparameterization is easy and it would have been considered plagiarism. See [1].

[1] Fangyu Zou, Li Shen, Zequn Jie, Weizhong Zhang, and Wei Liu. A sufficient condition for convergences of Adam and RMSprop. Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2019 - Also found here arxiv preprint arXiv:1811.09358, 2018.
(There you will see that the proposed theory assumes any \beta_t over iterations t, as long as beta_t's < 1, but there is no discussion about a specific sequence of beta_t's that work well in practice).

We note that the purpose of Demon is to provide a practical rule for gradient based + momentum optimizers, in order to lessen the burden of hyperparameter tuning. The additional theoretical guarantees we provide in the paper is to also cover the question "but there are no theoretical guarantees". Further, we note that, to the best of our knowledge, there are no convergence guarantees of optimizers for neural networks, unless someone makes strong assumptions on the simplicity of the problem considered (e.g., you can follow the work of Mahdi Soltanolkotabi, Jason Lee, Simon Du or Quanquan Gu - and others - for simplified scenarios). Recently, there are works that consider deeper architectures (see Quanquan Gu or Simon Du works), but we have to note that for each different architecture, one needs to use different theoretical techniques (each one of which could be an individual contribution). 

"The proposed ... show such results."

Many SOTA results with SGDM hinge on a fixed learning rate decay schedule which requires knowing the total iterations T before running. We follow this to achieve good results. When we run SGDM with learning rate decay on plateau, results for SGDM are worse which then misrepresents our Demon results as even better. Furthermore, our results on Adam show that Demon typically empirically strictly improves Adam, so even a rough estimate of T would improve its performance. We also want to emphasize that it is usual to have a somewhat good idea of how many iterations need to be run. For example, one of the most common situations in industry is to retrain existing networks frequently to account for data distribution shifts. That being said, we have results of comparing Demon with other momentum decay schedules, and find that Demon is significantly better, see Table 18 in Appendix G.

"The authors claimed ... evidence in experiments?"

We've provided heatmaps for several settings where we sweep over the hyperparameters (see Section 5.1). The Demon variants have a substantially larger band of light color, which indicates robustness to hyperparamter tuning. The results are also better than at first glance, since having a larger band of light color in both axes leads to a substantially larger number of hyperparameters for good performance, in some cases double the number of settings.

We hope these will change the reviewer's point of view about our contributions.
